consensus_summary: The ship primarily symbolizes the Church as the vessel of salvation that carries believers safely through worldly storms and judgment, based on Noah’s ark typology, the Gospel boat narratives with Jesus, and longstanding patristic/liturgical tradition.
book_summary: The ship symbolizes an earthly kingdom, city, state, or governed political body riding the sea of peoples, crewed by its inhabitants, guided by rulers, defended by armies, and loaded with wealth as cargo; Christ needs no such vessel, and the ship itself may break while its people survive.
boundary_disagreement: Consensus treats the ark and disciples’ boats as primary ecclesial images (with commercial ships of Tyre/Babylon as secondary illustrations of pride or wealth); the book elevates political/commercial ships as the sole core referent and reinterprets or brackets the Gospel/ark cases by stressing that Christ walks the sea without a ship and that vessels can be destroyed while people live.
material_contradiction: The consensus core equates ship with the Church; the book equates it with earthly political entities and explicitly distances Christ from any need for a constructed vessel, so both cannot be the primary identification of the same symbol.
rationale: Minimum cores are incompatible: Church-as-vessel versus earthly kingdom/city/state. Accepting the book’s identification requires replacing the consensus primary rather than merely narrowing or broadening a shared category. Consensus alternatives mention commerce or worldly power but keep them secondary and non-contradictory to the ecclesial reading; the book inverts that hierarchy and rejects the Church equation, producing core divergence.
strongest_objection: The entry omits the Gospel storm narratives and Noah-ark typology that form the historical backbone of the ship-as-Church consensus, relying only on judgment texts that the consensus already treats as secondary.
